claim: Neural synchrony generates fast network oscillations throughout the brain, including the main olfactory bulb (MOB), the first processing station of the olfactory system.
source: Neural synchrony generates fast network oscillations throughout the brain, including the main olfactory bulb (MOB), the first processing station of the olfactory system.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neural synchrony and the MOB's role in the olfactory system.

claim: Tufted cells (TCs) robustly synchronized across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies.
source: TCs robustly synchronized across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, while MC synchrony was weaker and concentrated in slow-gamma frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings and optogenetic activation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Mitral cell (MC) synchrony was weaker and concentrated in slow-gamma frequencies.
source: TCs robustly synchronized across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, while MC synchrony was weaker and concentrated in slow-gamma frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings comparing MCs to TCs.

claim: Synchrony among both cell types was enhanced by shared glomerular input.
source: Synchrony among both cell types was enhanced by shared glomerular input but was independent of intraglomerular lateral excitation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing homotypic and heterotypic cell pairs.

claim: Synchrony among both cell types was independent of intraglomerular lateral excitation.
source: Synchrony among both cell types was enhanced by shared glomerular input but was independent of intraglomerular lateral excitation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that TCs exhibited robust synchrony without lateral excitation.

claim: Cell-type differences in synchrony could not be traced to any difference in the synchronization of synaptic inhibition.
source: Cell-type differences in synchrony could also not be traced to any difference in the synchronization of synaptic inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recordings of inhibitory postsynaptic currents showing no cell-type differences in inhibitory synchronization.

claim: Greater TC than MC synchrony paralleled the more periodic firing among resonant TCs than MCs.
source: Instead, greater TC than MC synchrony paralleled the more periodic firing among resonant TCs than MCs and emerged in patterns consistent with densely synchronous network oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of spike-time auto-power spectral density and CV2 measurements showing greater periodicity in TC firing.

claim: TC and MC synchrony emerged in patterns consistent with densely synchronous network oscillations.
source: Instead, greater TC than MC synchrony paralleled the more periodic firing among resonant TCs than MCs and emerged in patterns consistent with densely synchronous network oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by data showing close correspondence between instantaneous firing rates and periodic synchrony frequencies.

claim: Gamma-frequency (~40–100 Hz) oscillations in the MOB reflect the synchronous firing of principal cells and are intimately linked with olfactory learning, memory, and behavior.
source: Fast network oscillations are widespread in neural activity throughout the mammalian brain, including the main olfactory bulb (MOB), where gamma-frequency (~40–100 Hz) oscillations reflecting the synchronous firing of principal cells are intimately linked with olfactory learning, memory, and behavior (Martin and Ravel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Martin and Ravel, 2014.

claim: TCs differ from MCs in their intrinsic and synaptic properties, sensory responses, and axonal projections.
source: Overwhelming evidence has established that TCs, a second type of excitatory MOB principal cell, differ from MCs in their intrinsic and synaptic properties, sensory responses, and axonal projections (Shepherd et al., 2004; Nagayama et al., 2014; Burton et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Shepherd et al., 2004; Nagayama et al., 2014; Burton et al., 2020.

claim: TCs and MCs form parallel pathways encoding complementary information.
source: Not only do these findings support a model in which TCs and MCs form parallel pathways encoding complementary information, but they further suggest that TCs and MCs may differentially engage in fast network oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the established differences between TCs and MCs.

claim: Weaker lateral inhibition among TCs than MCs suggests that TCs may synchronize less than MCs.
source: In particular, weaker lateral inhibition among TCs than MCs (Christie et al., 2001; Geramita et al., 2016) suggests that TCs may synchronize less than MCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings about lateral inhibition differences, cited from Christie et al., 2001; Geramita et al., 2016.

claim: Fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB are differentially modulated by state.
source: Fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB are differentially modulated by state (Kay, 2003; Frederick et al., 2016; Zhuang et al., 2019), suggesting both behavioral relevance and at least partially distinct underlying sources.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Kay, 2003; Frederick et al., 2016; Zhuang et al., 2019.

claim: The temporal sequencing of fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations across early and late phases of the sniff cycle parallels early and late sensory-evoked TC and MC firing.
source: Indeed, the temporal sequencing of fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations across early and late phases of the sniff cycle (Lepousez and Lledo, 2013; Manabe and Mori, 2013; Frederick et al., 2016), paralleling early and late sensory-evoked TC and MC firing, has motivated the attractive but untested hypothesis that TCs and MCs synchronize across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, respectively (Manabe and Mori, 2013; Mori et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Lepousez and Lledo, 2013; Manabe and Mori, 2013; Frederick et al., 2016.

claim: There is an untested hypothesis that TCs and MCs synchronize across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, respectively.
source: Indeed, the temporal sequencing of fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations across early and late phases of the sniff cycle (Lepousez and Lledo, 2013; Manabe and Mori, 2013; Frederick et al., 2016), paralleling early and late sensory-evoked TC and MC firing, has motivated the attractive but untested hypothesis that TCs and MCs synchronize across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, respectively (Manabe and Mori, 2013; Mori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an untested hypothesis from previous literature.

claim: A large population of granule cell (GC) interneurons mediate lateral inhibition among MOB principal cells.
source: A large population of granule cell (GC) interneurons mediate lateral inhibition among MOB principal cells, and several studies have proposed that periodic GC-mediated inhibition opens windows of opportunity for a subset of MCs to synchronously fire across a sparse fraction of gamma-frequency cycles (i.e., a sparsely synchronous oscillation or 'sparse synchrony') (Rall and Shepherd, 1968; Eeckman and Freeman, 1990; Neville and Haberly, 2003; Bathellier et al., 2006; Schoppa, 2006), paralleling pyramidal-interneuron gamma (PING) theories elsewhere in the brain (Wang, 2010; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Periodic GC-mediated inhibition opens windows of opportunity for a subset of MCs to synchronously fire across a sparse fraction of gamma-frequency cycles.
source: A large population of granule cell (GC) interneurons mediate lateral inhibition among MOB principal cells, and several studies have proposed that periodic GC-mediated inhibition opens windows of opportunity for a subset of MCs to synchronously fire across a sparse fraction of gamma-frequency cycles (i.e., a sparsely synchronous oscillation or 'sparse synchrony') (Rall and Shepherd, 1968; Eeckman and Freeman, 1990; Neville and Haberly, 2003; Bathellier et al., 2006; Schoppa, 2006), paralleling pyramidal-interneuron gamma (PING) theories elsewhere in the brain (Wang, 2010; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is a theory proposed in previous studies, supported by citations to Rall and Shepherd, 1968; Eeckman and Freeman, 1990; Neville and Haberly, 2003; Bathellier et al., 2006; Schoppa, 2006.

claim: Alternative theories point toward the capacity of correlated synaptic currents to reset the phase of resonant neural oscillators, synchronizing periodic firing across several consecutive gamma-frequency cycles.
source: Alternative theories, however, instead point toward the capacity of correlated synaptic currents, independent of periodicity, to reset the phase of resonant neural oscillators, synchronizing periodic firing across several consecutive gamma-frequency cycles (i.e., 'dense synchrony') (Desmaisons et al., 1999; Galán et al., 2006; Rubin and Cleland, 2006; David et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an alternative theory supported by citations to Desmaisons et al., 1999; Galán et al., 2006; Rubin and Cleland, 2006; David et al., 2015.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evoked ~20 Hz firing in MCs on average.
source: Such multiglomerular activation evoked ~20 Hz firing in MCs on average (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), with MCs of a pair occasionally firing synchronously (|Δtspike| ≤ 5 ms) (Figure 1A and D), similar to previous investigation of spike-time synchrony in MC pairs using electrical OSN stimulation (Schoppa, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Under identical conditions, multiglomerular activation evoked more rapid TC firing than MC firing.
source: Under identical conditions, multiglomerular activation evoked more rapid TC firing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H) and a remarkable degree of TC spike-time synchrony (Figure 1G and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evoked a remarkable degree of TC spike-time synchrony.
source: Under identical conditions, multiglomerular activation evoked more rapid TC firing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H) and a remarkable degree of TC spike-time synchrony (Figure 1G and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and J.

claim: Spike-time cross-correlograms among TCs exhibited prominent central peaks compared to minimal peaks among MCs.
source: Consistent with visual inspection of cell-attached traces, spike-time cross-correlograms among TCs exhibited prominent central peaks (|Δtspike| ≤ 5 ms) compared to minimal peaks among MCs (Figure 1B, E, H and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, E, H and K.

claim: Simulated spike trains generated from independent Poisson processes with rates matching experimental firing rate patterns replicated the slow-timescale correlations observed in TC spike times but failed to replicate the prominent cross-correlogram central peaks.
source: Excluding this possibility, however, simulated spike trains generated from independent Poisson processes with rates matching experimental firing rate patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) replicated the slow-timescale correlations observed in TC spike times but failed to replicate the prominent cross-correlogram central peaks (Figure 1B, E, H and K).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental and simulated data shown in Figure 1B, E, H and K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isolating fast-timescale synchrony exceeding chance levels revealed markedly higher central peaks among TCs than MCs.
source: Indeed, isolating fast-timescale synchrony exceeding chance levels (by subtracting simulated from experimental spike-time cross-correlograms) revealed markedly higher central peaks among TCs than MCs (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evokes greater spike-time synchrony among TCs than MCs independent of firing rate differences.
source: Multiglomerular activation thus evokes greater spike-time synchrony among TCs than MCs independent of firing rate differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing TCs and MCs after accounting for firing rate differences.

claim: TC pairs exhibited consistently higher CPSD levels overall, indicative of more precise spike-time synchrony.
source: Specifically, TC pairs exhibited consistently higher CPSD levels overall, indicative of more precise spike-time synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by spike-time CPSD analysis shown in the figures.

claim: TC firing synchronized across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, often with a sweeping deceleration across each photostimulation cycle.
source: Moreover, TC firing synchronized across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, often with a sweeping deceleration across each photostimulation cycle, while MC synchrony was less dynamic and largely limited to slow-gamma frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by spike-time CPSD spectrograms shown in the figures.

claim: MC synchrony was less dynamic and largely limited to slow-gamma frequencies.
source: Moreover, TC firing synchronized across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, often with a sweeping deceleration across each photostimulation cycle, while MC synchrony was less dynamic and largely limited to slow-gamma frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by spike-time CPSD spectrograms shown in the figures.

claim: 92% of recorded TC pairs exhibited ≥1 CPSD ridge compared to only 31% of MC pairs.
source: With this approach, 92%of recorded TC pairs exhibited ≥1 CPSD ridge compared to only 31%of MC pairs (Figure 1O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: TCs exhibited both more precise and higher frequency periodic synchrony than MCs.
source: Even when restricting our analysis to only those pairs exhibiting CPSD ridges, however, fundamental differences remained (Figure 1P), with TCs exhibiting both more precise and higher frequency periodic synchrony than MCs (Figure 1Q and R, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1P, Q, R, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Epochs of periodic spike-time synchrony were identified almost exclusively within gamma frequencies.
source: Of note, while we searched for CPSD ridges across a wide frequency range, epochs of periodic spike-time synchrony were nevertheless identified almost exclusively within gamma frequencies (Figure 1Q), highlighting the marked tuning of MOB circuitry to gamma-frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: Periodic synchronization at fast-gamma frequencies consistently emerged early in each photostimulation cycle, and decelerated toward slower gamma frequencies at mean rates up to 0.1–0.2 Hz/ms.
source: Additionally, while individual pairs exhibited variable ridge dynamics, periodic synchronization at fast-gamma frequencies consistently emerged early in each photostimulation cycle, and decelerated toward slower gamma frequencies at mean rates up to 0.1–0.2 Hz/ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both TC and MC spike-time synchrony persisted at levels higher than expected by chance throughout the average photostimulation cycle.
source: However, even under a barrage of predominantly asynchronous inhibitory synaptic input (see below) and following pauses in firing in one or both cells of a pair (e.g., Figure 1G and J), both TC and MC spike-time synchrony persisted at levels higher than expected by chance throughout the average photostimulation cycle (i.e., up to 200 ms following photostimulation) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Greater TC than MC spike-time synchrony persisted throughout the entire photostimulation cycle.
source: Cross-correlogram and CPSD ridge analyses further demonstrated that greater TC than MC spike-time synchrony likewise persisted throughout the entire photostimulation cycle (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The rates and temporal patterning of firing recorded closely match the odor-evoked firing observed in morphologically confirmed MCs and TCs in vivo.
source: Of further note, both the rates and temporal patterning of firing recorded closely match the odor-evoked firing observed in morphologically confirmed MCs and TCs in vivo (Nagayama et al., 2004; Igarashi et al., 2012; Phillips et al., 2012) (and see Discussion), confirming that our optogenetic approach recapitulates key aspects of MOB sensory processing.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous in vivo studies cited as Nagayama et al., 2004; Igarashi et al., 2012; Phillips et al., 2012.

claim: TCs and MCs exhibited comparable peak excitatory current amplitudes.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings obtained from a large subset of pairs following cell-attached recordings additionally revealed no cell-type difference in excitatory current amplitude and even modestly greater excitatory charge transferred to MCs than TCs throughout the photostimulation protocol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: MCs exhibited greater excitatory charge transferred throughout each photostimulation cycle than TCs.
source: Voltage-clamp recordings obtained from a large subset of pairs following cell-attached recordings additionally revealed no cell-type difference in excitatory current amplitude and even modestly greater excitatory charge transferred to MCs than TCs throughout the photostimulation protocol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Latencies from photostimulation onset to excitatory input were similar across cells of each pair among both MCs and TCs but across all pairs were fairly broadly distributed across ~10–25 ms.
source: Moreover, latencies from photostimulation onset to excitatory input were similar across cells of each pair among both MCs and TCs but across all pairs were fairly broadly distributed across ~10–25 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E), consistent with our optogenetic approach triggering more gradual and physiological glomerular activation than single or short bursts of electrical stimuli (Carey et al., 2009; Burton and Urban, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E, and citations to Carey et al., 2009; Burton and Urban, 2015.

claim: Excitatory input was completely devoid of any gamma-frequency patterning.
source: Excitatory input was also completely devoid of any gamma-frequency patterning (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), further arguing that the periodic spike-time synchrony observed was not directly driven by the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The dataset included more homotypic TC than MC pairs, but the proportion of homotypic to heterotypic pairs did not significantly differ between cell types.
source: While our dataset indeed included more homotypic TC than MC pairs, the proportion of homotypic to heterotypic pairs did not significantly differ between cell types (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Clear cell-type differences in periodic spike-time synchrony remained even when restricting analysis to homotypic or heterotypic pairs alone.
source: Moreover, clear cell-type differences in periodic spike-time synchrony remained even when restricting our analysis to homotypic or heterotypic pairs alone (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony fundamentally differs between MCs and TCs independent of glomerular organization.
source: Gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony thus fundamentally differs between MCs and TCs independent of glomerular organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing homotypic and heterotypic pairs.

claim: Spike-time CPSD ridges were detected in both homotypic and heterotypic pairs at comparable rates and across largely overlapping frequencies.
source: Spike-time CPSD ridges were detected in both homotypic and heterotypic pairs at comparable rates and across largely overlapping frequencies (Figure 3C and D), further arguing that the cell-type differences in gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony were not driven by differences in glomerular organization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Synchrony was markedly stronger across homotypic than heterotypic pairs.
source: Synchrony was, however, markedly stronger across homotypic than heterotypic pairs (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: Homotypic TCs exhibited no lateral excitation.
source: Surprisingly, this enhancement of spike-time synchrony occurred independent of intraglomerular lateral excitation, as homotypic TCs – which displayed robust periodic spike-time synchrony (Figure 1G and J, Figure 3B) – exhibited no lateral excitation, while 100%of the homotypic MC pairs tested exhibited typically asymmetric lateral excitation matching previous accounts (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: 100% of the homotypic MC pairs tested exhibited typically asymmetric lateral excitation.
source: Surprisingly, this enhancement of spike-time synchrony occurred independent of intraglomerular lateral excitation, as homotypic TCs – which displayed robust periodic spike-time synchrony (Figure 1G and J, Figure 3B) – exhibited no lateral excitation, while 100%of the homotypic MC pairs tested exhibited typically asymmetric lateral excitation matching previous accounts (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Lack of lateral excitation among TCs was not due to cell-type differences in electrical coupling, as homotypic MCs and homotypic TCs exhibited comparable electrical coupling coefficients.
source: Lack of lateral excitation among TCs was not due to cell-type differences in electrical coupling, however, as homotypic MCs and homotypic TCs exhibited comparable electrical coupling coefficients (Figure 3I), as previously reported (Ma and Lowe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and citation to Ma and Lowe, 2010.

claim: Some aspect of intraglomerular signaling – likely including electrical coupling – enhances fast network oscillations in the MOB.
source: Our data thus support the hypothesis that some aspect of intraglomerular signaling – likely including electrical coupling – enhances fast network oscillations in the MOB (Pouille et al., 2017), and further suggest that lateral excitation between homotypic MCs does not enhance (and may even hinder) periodic spike-time synchrony (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to Pouille et al., 2017.

claim: Lateral excitation between homotypic MCs does not enhance (and may even hinder) periodic spike-time synchrony.
source: Our data thus support the hypothesis that some aspect of intraglomerular signaling – likely including electrical coupling – enhances fast network oscillations in the MOB (Pouille et al., 2017), and further suggest that lateral excitation between homotypic MCs does not enhance (and may even hinder) periodic spike-time synchrony (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the experimental data showing TCs have robust synchrony without lateral excitation.

claim: TC pairs exhibited significantly shorter lateral intersomatic distances than MC pairs, despite equal total intersomatic distances.
source: TC pairs in our dataset indeed exhibited significantly shorter lateral intersomatic distances (i.e., distances parallel to the MCL) than MC pairs, despite equal total intersomatic distances (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Total and lateral intersomatic distance failed to correlate with cross-correlogram or CPSD measures of spike-time synchrony among TCs.
source: Total and lateral intersomatic distance failed to correlate with cross-correlogram or CPSD measures of spike-time synchrony among TCs, however, while MCs exhibited only a modest reduction in spike-time CPSD levels with increasing lateral intersomatic distance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: MCs exhibited only a modest reduction in spike-time CPSD levels with increasing lateral intersomatic distance.
source: Total and lateral intersomatic distance failed to correlate with cross-correlogram or CPSD measures of spike-time synchrony among TCs, however, while MCs exhibited only a modest reduction in spike-time CPSD levels with increasing lateral intersomatic distance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Differences in somatic depth failed to correlate with spike-time synchrony among TCs.
source: Similarly, while we recorded from TCs spanning the full depth of the external plexiform layer (EPL), differences in somatic depth also failed to correlate with spike-time synchrony among TCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evokes robust, widespread, and enduring synchronization of TC firing across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies.
source: In summary, our results thus demonstrate that multiglomerular activation evokes robust, widespread, and enduring synchronization of TC firing across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies and limited synchronization of MC firing primarily across slow-gamma frequencies, revealing fundamental cell-type differences that emerge across multiple analyses and cannot be explained by experimental or anatomical factors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evokes limited synchronization of MC firing primarily across slow-gamma frequencies.
source: In summary, our results thus demonstrate that multiglomerular activation evokes robust, widespread, and enduring synchronization of TC firing across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies and limited synchronization of MC firing primarily across slow-gamma frequencies, revealing fundamental cell-type differences that emerge across multiple analyses and cannot be explained by experimental or anatomical factors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The limited spike-time synchrony detected among MCs constrains extensive characterization of the frequency of periodic MC synchronization.
source: As a caveat, the limited spike-time synchrony detected among MCs in our dataset constrains extensive characterization of the frequency of periodic MC synchronization.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the data.

claim: The results do not exclude a contribution of MC spike-time synchrony to fast-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB.
source: Our results thus do not exclude a contribution of MC spike-time synchrony to fast-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about what the results do not rule out.

claim: The results definitively identify robust periodic spike-time synchrony among TCs as a major contributor to fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB.
source: However, our results do definitively identify robust periodic spike-time synchrony among TCs as a major contributor to fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB, as reflected by the marked resemblance of TC spike-time CPSD spectrograms to LFP spectrograms recorded in the MOB of freely behaving rodents (compare Figure 4 to Figure 2 of Manabe and Mori, 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to in vivo LFP recordings from Manabe and Mori, 2013.

claim: TC spike-time CPSD spectrograms markedly resemble LFP spectrograms recorded in the MOB of freely behaving rodents.
source: However, our results do definitively identify robust periodic spike-time synchrony among TCs as a major contributor to fast- and slow-gamma-frequency oscillations in the MOB, as reflected by the marked resemblance of TC spike-time CPSD spectrograms to LFP spectrograms recorded in the MOB of freely behaving rodents (compare Figure 4 to Figure 2 of Manabe and Mori, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of Figure 4 to Figure 2 of Manabe and Mori, 2013.

claim: TC firing exhibited substantially greater synchronization across theta frequencies than MC firing.
source: In addition to pronounced gamma-frequency synchrony, TC firing also exhibited substantially greater synchronization across theta frequencies than MC firing (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sensory information specifically encoded in the cross-frequency coupling of MOB gamma- and theta-frequency oscillations is conveyed to downstream olfactory cortical areas by synchronous TC firing.
source: Our results thus additionally suggest that sensory information specifically encoded in the cross-frequency coupling of MOB gamma- and theta-frequency oscillations (Buonviso et al., 2006; Schaefer and Margrie, 2007; Mori et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2017; Tort et al., 2018; Heck et al., 2019; Losacco et al., 2020) is conveyed to downstream olfactory cortical areas by synchronous TC firing.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work on cross-frequency coupling.

claim: 2 Hz and 8 Hz photostimulation evoked qualitatively similar patterns of periodic spike-time synchrony as 5 Hz photostimulation in a subset of TC pairs.
source: Moreover, while we did not systematically examine photostimulation across other theta frequencies associated with rodent olfaction, in a subset of TC pairs we confirmed that 2 Hz and 8 Hz photostimulation evoked qualitatively similar patterns of periodic spike-time synchrony as 5 Hz photostimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed cell-type differences in spike-time synchrony generalize across different olfactory sampling strategies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed cell-type differences in spike-time synchrony generalize across different olfactory sampling strategies.
source: Moreover, while we did not systematically examine photostimulation across other theta frequencies associated with rodent olfaction, in a subset of TC pairs we confirmed that 2 Hz and 8 Hz photostimulation evoked qualitatively similar patterns of periodic spike-time synchrony as 5 Hz photostimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the observed cell-type differences in spike-time synchrony generalize across different olfactory sampling strategies.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the experimental data from different photostimulation frequencies.

claim: Multiglomerular activation evoked a prolonged barrage of inhibitory input to both MCs and TCs.
source: Multiglomerular activation evoked a prolonged barrage of inhibitory input to both MCs and TCs (Figure 6A, D, G and J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with increases in IPSC rate and amplitude and a decrease in IPSC decay constant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, D, G, J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, 2.

claim: No differences in IPSC rise-time or decay constant were observed between cell types.
source: Though IPSC kinetics can influence fast network oscillations in the MOB (Lagier et al., 2007; Lepousez and Lledo, 2013), no differences in IPSC rise-time or decay constant were observed between cell types (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: Evoked IPSC rates were higher in MCs than TCs.
source: Evoked IPSC rates were, however, higher in MCs than TCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), consistent with stronger lateral and feedforward inhibition among MCs than TCs (Christie et al., 2001; Geramita and Urban, 2016; Geramita et al., 2016; Geramita and Urban, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and citations to previous work.

claim: Many IPSCs were synchronized in both MC pairs and TC pairs.
source: Within the barrage of synaptic inhibition, many IPSCs were indeed synchronized in both MC pairs and TC pairs (Figure 6A, D, G and J), and cross-correlograms of IPSC times revealed prominent central peaks in both cell types (Figure 6B, E, H and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, D, G, J, B, E, H, K.

claim: There was no cell-type difference in central peak heights of IPSC-time cross-correlograms.
source: Surprisingly, despite the marked differences in spike-time synchrony, there was no cell-type difference in central peak heights of IPSC-time cross-correlograms (Figure 6M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6M.

claim: Multiglomerular activation does not evoke more synchronous inhibition among TCs than MCs.
source: Multiglomerular activation thus does not evoke more synchronous inhibition among TCs than MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IPSC synchrony.

claim: Neither the relative rate nor amplitude of synchronous to asynchronous IPSCs was greater among TCs than MCs.
source: Critically, however, neither the relative rate nor amplitude of synchronous to asynchronous IPSCs was greater among TCs than MCs.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of synchronous and asynchronous IPSCs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Varying the time window within which evoked IPSCs were classified as synchronous yielded a consistently larger fraction of synchronous IPSCs among MCs than TCs.
source: Moreover, varying the time window within which evoked IPSCs were classified as synchronous (wIPSC), thus providing a measure of synchrony precision (Schoppa, 2006), yielded a consistently larger fraction of synchronous IPSCs (Fsynch) among MCs than TCs (Figure 6O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6O.

claim: The greater synchronization of TC than MC firing does not emerge from more synchronous synaptic inhibition among TCs than MCs.
source: Our results thus firmly establish that the greater synchronization of TC than MC firing does not emerge from more synchronous synaptic inhibition among TCs than MCs, refuting our first hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IPSC synchrony.

claim: Periodic synchronization of IPSC times was weaker, spread across a broader frequency range, and less concentrated into distinct epochs than periodic spike-time synchrony.
source: While multiglomerular activation indeed evoked a visible increase in IPSC-time synchrony across fast frequencies in both cell types (Figure 6C, F, I and L), this increase was fundamentally distinct from the increase observed in spike-time synchrony. In particular, periodic synchronization of IPSC times was weaker, spread across a broader frequency range, and less concentrated into distinct epochs than periodic spike-time synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, F, I, L.

claim: The modest increase in periodic synchronization of IPSC times in both cell types could be attributed entirely to an increase in chance levels of synchrony with increasing IPSC rates.
source: CPSD analysis of simulated IPSC times generated from independent Poisson processes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) in fact revealed that the modest increase in periodic synchronization of IPSC times in both cell types could be attributed entirely to an increase in chance levels of synchrony with increasing IPSC rates (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental and simulated IPSC-time CPSD shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cell-type differences in gamma-frequency synchronization of synaptic inhibition do not account for the dynamic synchronization of TC firing across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies and the more stable synchronization of MC firing at slow-gamma frequencies.
source: Cell-type differences in gamma-frequency synchronization of synaptic inhibition thus do not account for the dynamic synchronization of TC firing across fast- and slow-gamma frequencies and the more stable synchronization of MC firing at slow-gamma frequencies, refuting our second hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on IPSC synchrony.

claim: Differences in synaptic inhibition among TCs and MCs do not underlie the cell-type differences in gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony.
source: In summary, our results thus show that differences in synaptic inhibition among TCs and MCs do not underlie the cell-type differences in gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on synaptic inhibition.

claim: The minimal gamma-frequency synchrony in inhibitory inputs stands in stark contrast to the precise gamma-frequency synchronization of synaptic excitation and inhibition observed during fast network oscillations driven by temporal gating elsewhere in the brain.
source: Together with the lack of gamma-frequency synchrony in excitatory inputs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), the minimal gamma-frequency synchrony in inhibitory inputs stands in stark contrast to the precise gamma-frequency synchronization of synaptic excitation and inhibition observed during fast network oscillations driven by temporal gating elsewhere in the brain (e.g., Whittington et al., 1995; Fisahn et al., 1998; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Atallah and Scanziani, 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings in other brain regions, supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic inhibition remains a necessary component of fast network oscillations in the MOB.
source: Consequently, while synaptic inhibition remains a necessary component of fast network oscillations in the MOB, some other cellular or circuit feature must account for the profound differences observed in periodic synchronization of TC and MC firing, motivating consideration of alternative mechanisms of gamma-frequency synchrony.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and previous knowledge about the role of inhibition.

claim: Both MCs and TCs exhibited more periodic gamma-frequency firing than rate-matched Poisson processes.
source: Both MCs and TCs exhibited more periodic gamma-frequency firing than rate-matched Poisson processes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), with cell-type differences in APSD spectrograms closely matching the cell-type differences in CPSD spectrograms among pairs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TCs exhibited highly periodic firing across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies.
source: Specifically, TCs exhibited highly periodic firing across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, while MCs exhibited less periodic firing across predominantly slow-gamma frequencies (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: MCs exhibited less periodic firing across predominantly slow-gamma frequencies.
source: Specifically, TCs exhibited highly periodic firing across both fast- and slow-gamma frequencies, while MCs exhibited less periodic firing across predominantly slow-gamma frequencies (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: 85% of TCs exhibited ≥1 APSD ridge compared to only 44% of MCs.
source: Indeed, maximal ridge detection using a threshold (λ) equal to the 95th percentile of 40–200 Hz APSD values across all cells confirmed that 85%of TCs exhibited ≥1 APSD ridge compared to only 44%of MCs (Figure 7E), with epochs of robust periodic firing among TCs extending across higher frequencies and APSD levels than MCs (Figure 7G–I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Epochs of robust periodic firing among TCs extended across higher frequencies and APSD levels than MCs.
source: Indeed, maximal ridge detection using a threshold (λ) equal to the 95th percentile of 40–200 Hz APSD values across all cells confirmed that 85%of TCs exhibited ≥1 APSD ridge compared to only 44%of MCs (Figure 7E), with epochs of robust periodic firing among TCs extending across higher frequencies and APSD levels than MCs (Figure 7G–I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G–I, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Greater TC than MC oscillatory behavior persisted throughout the average photostimulation cycle.
source: Greater TC than MC oscillatory behavior further persisted throughout the average photostimulation cycle (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: TC firing exhibited lower median CV2 values throughout the photostimulation protocol than MC firing.
source: Indeed, across all cells, median CV2 was significantly lower among TCs than MCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Despite the more phasic firing pattern of TCs than MCs, TC firing remained more periodic from moment to moment than MC firing.
source: Thus, despite the more phasic firing pattern of TCs than MCs, TC firing remained more periodic from moment to moment than MC firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CV2 analysis.

claim: TCs exhibit greater gamma-frequency firing periodicity than MCs.
source: Together with the above spectral analysis, these results confirm that TCs exhibit greater gamma-frequency firing periodicity than MCs, consistent with our first hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the APSD and CV2 analyses.

claim: Epochs of robust periodic spike-time synchrony were almost exclusively detected among periodic pairs.
source: Strikingly, epochs of robust periodic spike-time synchrony, manifest in spike-time CPSD ridges, were almost exclusively detected among periodic pairs, independent of cell type (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Spike-time synchrony independent of periodicity was markedly greater among periodic than aperiodic pairs.
source: Spike-time synchrony independent of periodicity, as measured by cross-correlogram central peaks, was likewise markedly greater among periodic than aperiodic pairs (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Spike-time cross-correlogram central peaks directly correlated with spike-time APSD averaged throughout the photostimulation protocol in both MCs and TCs considered together or separately.
source: On a per-pair basis, spike-time cross-correlogram central peaks further directly correlated with spike-time APSD averaged throughout the photostimulation protocol in both MCs and TCs considered together or separately (Figure 7L–N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7L–N.

claim: Oscillatory behavior promotes spike-time synchrony in the MOB.
source: Oscillatory behavior thus promotes spike-time synchrony in the MOB, with TCs exhibiting greater gamma-frequency firing periodicity than MCs, confirming our first hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between oscillatory behavior and spike-time synchrony.

claim: The instantaneous firing rates of MCs and TCs specifically during epochs of robust periodic synchrony closely matched instantaneous CPSD ridge frequencies.
source: In contrast to these regions, the instantaneous firing rates of MCs and TCs specifically during epochs of robust periodic synchrony (i.e., spike-time CPSD ridges) instead closely matched instantaneous CPSD ridge frequencies (Figure 8A–E), with deviations largely limited to abrupt transitions in firing rate (e.g., immediately following photostimulation) that exceeded the finite resolution of our spectral analysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A–E.

claim: The mean correspondence between instantaneous firing rate and the frequency of periodic spike-time synchrony approached unity in both cell types.
source: Indeed, across all cells, the mean correspondence between instantaneous firing rate and the frequency of periodic spike-time synchrony approached unity in both cell types (Figure 8F), with TC firing extending into faster frequencies than MC firing to match the fast-gamma-frequency synchrony widely observed among TCs (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: TC firing extended into faster frequencies than MC firing to match the fast-gamma-frequency synchrony widely observed among TCs.
source: Indeed, across all cells, the mean correspondence between instantaneous firing rate and the frequency of periodic spike-time synchrony approached unity in both cell types (Figure 8F), with TC firing extending into faster frequencies than MC firing to match the fast-gamma-frequency synchrony widely observed among TCs (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Close correspondence between firing rate and periodic synchrony is indicative of spike-time synchrony across multiple consecutive oscillatory cycles.
source: Such close correspondence between firing rate and periodic synchrony – indicative of spike-time synchrony across multiple consecutive oscillatory cycles and particularly evident among TCs (Figure 1G and J) – directly agrees with dense spike-time synchrony arising from the phase-resetting of periodically firing neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on firing rate and synchrony correspondence.

claim: Relative firing rate differences were both lower within TC than MC pairs and negatively correlated with cross-correlogram and CPSD measures of spike-time synchrony.
source: Further supporting this conclusion, relative firing rate differences, which can attenuate phase-resetting-mediated synchronization (Burton et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2013), were both lower within TC than MC pairs and, independent of cell type, negatively correlated with cross-correlogram and CPSD measures of spike-time synchrony (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citations to Burton et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: The intrinsic biophysical properties of TCs yield greater tendency toward oscillatory behavior (i.e., resonance) than the biophysical properties of MCs.
source: That TCs exhibit greater oscillatory behavior than MCs despite comparable synaptic input following multiglomerular activation suggests that the intrinsic biophysical properties of TCs yield greater tendency toward oscillatory behavior (i.e., resonance) than the biophysical properties of MCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing greater TC oscillatory behavior despite comparable synaptic input.

claim: 92% of TCs were resonant compared to only 50% of MCs.
source: Applying our operational metric, 92%of TCs proved resonant compared to only 50%of MCs (Figure 9U).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9U.

claim: Subthreshold resonance is more widespread among TCs than MCs.
source: Subthreshold resonance is thus more widespread among TCs than MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of subthreshold oscillations.

claim: Among resonant TCs and MCs, nearly all cells exhibited robust phase-locking of spike times to the preceding STO.
source: Among resonant TCs and MCs, nearly all cells exhibited robust phase-locking of spike times to the preceding STO (Figure 9V).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9V.

claim: MC spikes consistently occurred at phases just prior to the STO peak.
source: MC spikes consistently occurred at phases just prior to the STO peak (Figure 9D), matching previous findings (Desmaisons et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D and citation to Desmaisons et al., 1999.

claim: TC spike times exhibited identical phase-locking to MCs, with no difference in mean spike phase observed between cell types.
source: TC spike times exhibited identical phase-locking (Figure 9N and S), with no difference in mean spike phase observed between cell types (Figure 9V).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9N, S, V.

claim: TC firing persisted at instantaneous rates closely matching STO frequencies.
source: Following the initial post-STO spike, however, TC firing persisted at instantaneous rates closely matching STO frequencies (Figure 9L, O, Q and T), while MC firing was visibly outpaced by the preceding STO (Figure 9B and E), a difference particularly evident at the population level (Figure 9W).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9L, O, Q, T.

claim: MC firing was visibly outpaced by the preceding STO.
source: Following the initial post-STO spike, however, TC firing persisted at instantaneous rates closely matching STO frequencies (Figure 9L, O, Q and T), while MC firing was visibly outpaced by the preceding STO (Figure 9B and E), a difference particularly evident at the population level (Figure 9W).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B, E.

claim: TCs exhibited a 1:1 relationship between firing rate and STO frequency while MCs exhibited a 1:2 relationship.
source: Indeed, across all resonant cells, TCs exhibited a 1:1 relationship between firing rate and STO frequency while MCs exhibited a 1:2 relationship (Figure 9W).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9W.

claim: Subthreshold resonance is not only more widespread among TCs than MCs, but it also more faithfully entrains TC than MC firing.
source: Subthreshold resonance is thus not only more widespread among TCs than MCs, but it also more faithfully entrains TC than MC firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of subthreshold oscillations and firing entrainment.

claim: These results implicate specific conductances involved in STO generation with the greater oscillatory behavior among TCs than MCs.
source: Critically, these results not only implicate specific conductances involved in STO generation with the greater oscillatory behavior among TCs than MCs (see Discussion), but additionally identify synchronization of STOs as a possible mechanism sustaining dense gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony across gaps in TC firing (e.g., Figure 1G and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on subthreshold oscillations.

claim: Synchronization of STOs is a possible mechanism sustaining dense gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony across gaps in TC firing.
source: Critically, these results not only implicate specific conductances involved in STO generation with the greater oscillatory behavior among TCs than MCs (see Discussion), but additionally identify synchronization of STOs as a possible mechanism sustaining dense gamma-frequency spike-time synchrony across gaps in TC firing (e.g., Figure 1G and J).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data on subthreshold oscillations.
